content.title: About
content.content: White confectioners' sugar (powdered sugar) is a finely ground crystalline sugar, often fortified with a small amount of starch to prevent caking. It is widely used in baking, for dusting pastries, and in the preparation of icings, frostings, and desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Powdered sugar gets its name from its fine, powder‑like texture.
About 3 % cornstarch is typically added to prevent clumping.
In the United States it is known as "confectioners' sugar," while in Russia it is called "сахарная пудра."
Its fine texture allows it to dissolve quickly, making it ideal for smooth icings without graininess.
The delicate dusting effect is often used to create a "snowfall" look on cakes.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: Sugar is rapidly absorbed, providing an immediate boost of glucose to the bloodstream.

items.title: Flavor enhancement
items.content: Small amounts of powdered sugar can amplify the perceived sweetness of other ingredients, improving overall taste.

items.title: Blood sugar spikes
items.content: Excessive consumption can lead to hyperglycemia and increase the risk of developing diabetes.

items.title: Dental caries
items.content: Sugar serves as a food source for oral bacteria that cause tooth enamel decay.

items.title: Starch allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to the added cornstarch and experience food intolerance.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Powdered sugar is used for dusting baked goods, making icings, frostings, marzipan, and in no‑bake recipes where rapid dissolution is desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store powdered sugar in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Moisture can cause it to cake; if this happens, sift before use.
